Buildings are often thought of as “silent witnesses of history”, but they have a history of talking, especially in moments of crisis. In a pamphlet published in London in 1641, at the height of the Reformation, two monuments that served as sites of Catholic devotion literally converse, trying to make sense of (and poke fun at) the Protestant vandalism against them.1 In the eighteenth century, a whole genre of texts developed in which authors imagined what buildings might have said if they could speak to each other or passersby.2

This was not just a matter for the popular press. The end of the eighteenth century saw the emergence of “architecture parlante” (speaking architecture), through a group of architects who argued that buildings ought to communicate their function and meaning to people, through figurative symbols, letters, or inscriptions.3 When opinions about a certain monument or a cityscape predominate, buildings must speak for themselves to set things straight. This happened through experimental designs by Claude-Nicolas Ledoux and others, but also through pamphlets, broadsheets, cartoons, and newspaper articles that were written for a broader public and gave voice to the built environment.4

In mid-nineteenth-century Athens, the furious construction of the new capital in the recently established Greek state produced a lot of new buildings, but little architectural theory. Academically trained architects in Athens may have been too busy designing, or too antagonistic and secretive, to share their theories in writing. But architectural criticism abounded in the popular press, often penned by anonymous authors and frequently satirical. On February 3, 1854, the Athenian newspaper Athena (Αθηνά) published an anonymous satirical text titled “A Dialogue between the Belfries of the Capital [Διάλογος των κωδωνοστασίων της Πρωτευούσης]”.5 In it, the belfries of Athens’ churches debate current affairs and the future of the city, acutely aware of the shifting geopolitics of Europe.

Athens had become the Greek capital two decades earlier, and was the epicentre of intensive building activity. Plans were drawn up to rebuild it on a rectangular grid and expand it on monumental axes.6 Its ancient sites were cleared of rubble and anything else that was seen as an obstruction, including Byzantine and Ottoman remains.7 Monumental neoclassical buildings were erected to house the country’s new institutions: a university, an academy, a library, a palace. . . The small Ottoman town of Athens was trying to transform itself into a European capital.

Hansen was commissioned by King Otto to design the National Library of Greece (left), University of Athens (centre), and Academy of Athens (right). The buildings were completed, respectively, in 1903, 1864, and 1887 — Source.

Given this aspiration, it is fitting that the “Dialogue” opens with the belfry of the Byzantine church of Taxiarchs, a modest eleventh-century chapel that stood next to the Roman Agora and would in later years be demolished,8 boasting with great confidence:

All the travellers that pass by here fix their eyes on me and admire me. Many say that, in the whole world, there are only three belfries worth talking about: the one of [Our Lady of] Tinos, the one of [the Cathedral of] Strasbourg, and me. . . . And I do not say this out of any vanity — the other day I saw an [English] lord who not only observed me with great curiosity, but also cried in admiration: “By Zeus! This belfry is worthy of being transported to the British Museum!” . . . What other building has ever heard such praise from the Enlightened world?9

In reality, few foreign travellers (whether onlookers or looters) or local authorities were interested in Greece’s Byzantine churches at that time.10 Systematic efforts for their protection would begin toward the end of the nineteenth century,11 but initially, these buildings received little attention,12 despite the ostensible existence of a law ordering the preservation of the Byzantine, Venetian, and Turkish “relics of the Middle Ages”.13 Many of these churches were left in disrepair or demolished to make way for new streets and buildings,14 or even reclaimed as material for the construction of new churches.15 A survey of Athens in 1833 documented a total of 115 churches, of which only 30 were deemed in a good enough condition to merit repairs; a survey made roughly a decade later indicated that only half of those survived.16

The Taxiarchs belfry’s braggadocio was ironic, of course, because like all the rest of post-Ottoman Athens’ churches, it was modest at best. Views of the city around 1800 — such as Edward Dodwell’s famous image of The Bazaar at Athens — show a skyline dominated by minarets, not bell towers. Christians living under Ottoman rule were only allowed to build or repair churches as long as their architecture did not compete with that of the mosques.17 In most cases, freestanding bell towers were not allowed. The old churches of Athens only had modest belfries, usually at the extension of an existing wall, where a single bell hung under an arched opening.

After the withdrawal of Ottoman forces from Athens in 1833, all of the city’s minarets were gradually demolished, along with many of its mosques. In the 1840s and 50s, a number of projects for the erection of new churches or the refurbishment of existing ones began to explore new architectural possibilities, styles, and typologies, some of which involved monumental, at times freestanding bell towers.18 It was precisely such a new construction that the belfries of the “Dialogue” were meeting to discuss.

The news is announced by the belfry of Saint Marina near Thisseion: carved into the rock of the Hill of the Nymphs, this minuscule thirteenth-century chapel was almost as obscure as the Taxiarchs, and, like it, was later demolished and replaced by a modern church.19

Saint Marina interrupts the Taxiarchs:

[Saint Marina:] Quiet down, brother, stop shouting. . . . Now comes the time when you will cease your bragging.

[Taxiarchs:] What are you talking about, my insignificant little belfry? Pardon me, I was unaware of your existence. Tell me, why and for whom should I cease?

[Saint Marina:] I heard . . . that a gleaming, tall and elegant belfry will soon be erected in our city.

[Taxiarchs:] Where, my little one, where? And it will be tall, you say?

[Saint Marina:] Yes! the old Nikodemos is planning to dazzle our eyes; he wants to make a child in his own image and likeness. Many say that this will be the most beautiful creature.

[Taxiarchs:] And tall, you say?

[Saint Marina:] I heard it will be tall, as tall as the sky. . .20

“Nikodemos” [Sotira Nikodemou, also known as Lykodemou] was an eleventh-century Byzantine church, whose complete refurbishment included the erection of a new, freestanding, four-storey bell tower, then an unprecedented novelty for the city. The church had been given to Athens’ expanding Russian community after a petition from Tsar Nicholas I. It was perhaps the popularity of neo-Byzantine architecture in the Russian Empire at the time that led to the bell tower being designed in imitation of the church it neighboured. The tower, completed in 1855, imitated the church’s distinctive details, from its brick-arched windows and cloisonné masonry to its pseudo-Kufic ornament and thin strips of ceramic dentils.21

Built with Russian funds, this flamboyant construction had important political implications. The Crimean War (1853–56) was in full swing, and Greece, ruled by the Bavarian-born King Otto, had found itself trapped between Europe’s Great Powers. Russia’s attack on the Ottoman Empire and its claim to defend the well-being of all Orthodox Christians living under the Sultan’s rule appealed to newly independent Greeks — some of whom were revanchists that dreamt of a Greek “reconquest” of Istanbul and the Hagia Sophia. However, England and France were applying their own pressure for Greece to withdraw. On May 12, 1854 (three months after the publication of the “Dialogue”, and while the restoration of the church was still under way), England and France occupied the port of Piraeus and the city of Athens, and forced King Otto to withdraw his troops from Ottoman territories and to declare Greece’s neutrality.

Accordingly, three less indigenous structures of Athens then join the conversation: the Clock Tower of Elgin in the Roman Agora, which was built in 1814 to accommodate a large clock gifted by Lord Elgin after he had looted the Parthenon marbles;22 the belfry of the recently completed neo-Gothic Anglican church on Philhellenon Street;23 and the belfry of the Catholic church of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite (“Saint Denis”) on Panepistimiou Avenue, whose slow construction had become a local joke.24 These three buildings personified foreign interests in Greece and the various foreign communities (Germans, Austrians, French, English, and Americans) and confessions (Catholics and Protestants) that had settled in Athens after 1830 and had funded their construction. Russian presence represented a threat to all these Western powers, and so the three foreign buildings fiercely oppose the project of the bell tower of Saint Nikodemos by appealing to local patriotic sentiment.

The Clock Tower of Elgin speaks first:

It’s a conspiracy! Thieves, robbers! Grab your arms, brothers! friends! neighbours! Look, we are perishing! rush to the rescue! . . . For the love of God, wake up! behold. . . our enemy. . . he is approaching, he is here... he captures us, he murders!25

The belfries of the Anglican church and Saint Denis join the chorus:

Do not let him approach!

When one of the local belfries asks them who that incoming enemy is, the Clock Tower of Elgin declares:

It’s the Moscov Giaour [sic: Ο Μοσκόβ Γκιαούρ].26

The Turkish word “giaour [gâvur]” was a derogatory Ottoman term for a non-Muslim, particularly a Christian. By putting this word in the mouth of the English tower, the author of the “Dialogue” hints at the true allegiance of these Western powers: not to the Greeks, whom they called “brothers” a moment ago, but to the Sultan.

For many Greek elites and the Bavarian-born monarchy, maintaining the alliance with these Western powers was a priority — Athens’ foreign communities needed to be accommodated. But the erection of new Protestant and Catholic churches was an affront to the local Orthodox population, who were receiving no new church of their own. In 1841, an anonymous newspaper columnist condemned “the unforgivable indifference” of the Greek government with regard to “building an [Orthodox] church . . . with sufficient capacity and the needed propriety” for official celebrations.27 Adding insult to injury, King Otto himself had remained Catholic on taking the throne. Although he attended Orthodox celebrations and even sponsored the erection of the city’s Metropolitan Cathedral (which would be completed in 1862), he had not received an Orthodox baptism. This did not sit well with many of his Greek subjects.

In this context, the pompous restoration of an old Byzantine church by the Orthodox Tsar of Russia would have certainly been welcomed by many Athenians — perhaps even by the anonymous author of the “Dialogue”. Still, all the Orthodox churches of the “Dialogue” do not form a unified front. The churches are riven by internal divides. Soon after the appearance of the two old Byzantine churches and the three Western structures, a modern Orthodox church enters the scene: Saint Eirini. Completed just four years earlier and serving at the time as the city’s Orthodox cathedral, Saint Eirini was a gleaming neo-Renaissance edifice, whose plastered and pedimented facade stood on one of the city’s first monumental avenues, Aiolou Street. Like the other Athenian churches, however, Saint Eirini lacked big bell towers: its bells hung on two relatively modest belfries over its facade. And so it also regards the new Russian bell tower with envy.

Ultimately, it is not confession but architectural form that determines the battle lines. When the Byzantine chapel of the Transfiguration of the Saviour at the foot of the Acropolis joins the chorus against the Russian tower, Saint Eirini scoffs:

What? You too . . . are speaking against [this tower]? When we say something against Nikodemos, anyone can easily conclude [that this stems] from our Italian character . . . but you, have you no shame? Both in name and in essence [ονόματι και πράγματι], you are truly a Russian belfry.28

For the neo-Renaissance Saint Eirini, the Byzantine architecture of this little chapel of the Transfiguration puts it in the same camp as Nikodemos. Many similar accusations were made in the “Dialogue”. When the neo-Gothic Anglican church joins the neo-Renaissance Saint Denis in shooing away their common enemy, the Byzantine church of Saint Marina accuses the former: “You have nothing in common with Saint Denis. You have our [i.e., Byzantine] form and, together with your church, you face the east [Συ και το σχήμα ημέτερον έχεις και μετά της εκκλησίας σου προς ανατολάς στρέφεις]”.29 The confusion in the accusations appears to be intentional: the author of the “Dialogue” was satirizing the chaos in the city around the classification of historical architectural styles, typologies, and genealogies.30

In the newly established Greek nation-state, whose nation-building discourse was almost exclusively based on classical antiquity, medieval diversions were often a matter of controversy. As Greek nation-builders were anxious to construct a narrative of uninterrupted continuity with classical antiquity in order to align themselves with the West, Byzantium was seen by many as a “dark”, “oriental” interval that was best left forgotten. However, King Otto was occasionally favourable to modern uses of the local Byzantine heritage. In 1846, he launched a competition for the design of the Athens Metropolitan Cathedral and urged that it be done in a “Greco-Byzantine [Ελληνοβυζαντινό]” style.31 The winning design, by local architect Demetrios Zezos — a mixture of Byzantine, Romanesque, and classicist features — was lauded by some32 but loathed by others; one enraged anonymous author wrote in an Athenian newspaper in 1857:

What a shame [for one] to see such architectural monstrosities [εξαμβλώματα αρχιτεκτονικής], such testaments of utter tastelessness. And where? In the city of Athens, next to the Propylaea, the Parthenon and the Erechtheion! It seems that we are trying to surpass the Byzantines in tastelessness, instead of using as our models the wonderful works of our immortal forefathers [i.e., the ancient Greeks].33

As the “Dialogue” unfolds, all these modern churches of Athens (both those of Western confessions and those in Western styles) eventually stop accusing each other and unite against Nikodemos, scrutinizing its architecture for incriminating details they could use to stop the construction. The first thing they notice is the orientation of the new structure. The tower had been placed parallel to the old church, which, like most older buildings, did not align with the new urban grid that was built around them. As a result, the Anglican church points out, the bell tower stood more or less at a 45-degree angle to the adjacent Philhellenon Street.

Yet they need more. Saint Eirini takes the lead, assuming a prosecutorial tone:

By God, why [should there be] such a tall belfry in our small and poor capital? What is the use for it? What are we, Turks, wanting minarets? [Μη γαρ ημείς Τούρκοι είμεθα και θέλομεν μιναρέδας;] . . . The ancient and sacred Acropolis is indignant about this sacrilegious novelty, and [Mount] Hymettus, from his top to his lowest foothills, has likely the same opinion.34

This is still not enough, so Saint Eirini continues:

My brothers and partners, you know that this monster has sprouted out of the ground like a mushroom, without following any kind of architecture, and stands, as is known, before the entrance of Nikodemos. It is also known that Hagia Sophia [in Istanbul] had her belfry placed similarly before her, but. . . why should we care about this Turkish mosque [τι μέλλει ημίν δια το Τουρκικόν αυτό τζαμίον]? The Queen of churches and the model for our Metropolitan Cathedral — that is, Saint Peter’s [in Rome] — has his facade open and free [of any such obstacles]. And so we all cry out that this monstrosity of Nikodemos is an inexcusable disproportion, a rape and an infection of the ancient Byzantine architecture — deafness, barbarism, nonsense, treachery ...chery ...ery ...ry, etc. [προδοσία ...σία ...ία ...α, κτλ].35

The echo of the last word — “προδοσία ...σία ...ία ...α” — adds to the comic effect, as we imagine Saint Eirini pompously rehearsing its speech in an empty hall. The addition of “etc.” at the end hints at the banality of it all despite the urgent tone: one can easily imagine the rest, the author of the “Dialogue” implies.

But something more interesting is taking place here: Saint Eirini brings in Hagia Sophia — an object of profound religious veneration and nationalist desire for most Greeks — but only to dismiss it as a “Turkish mosque”, and then to turn the audience’s attention to Saint Peter’s in Rome, which it deems the true model for the Metropolitan Cathedral of Athens (at the time under construction), even though the latter had evident Byzantine and Gothic features. As it mounts its argument, Saint Eirini often distorts historical facts but is consistent in embracing Western architectural models and in its fiery rejection of anything “oriental”.

Suddenly, a mysterious new character appears: the “Ideal Belfry [Κωδωνοστάσιον Ιδανικόν]”36, which interrupts the conversation with the “most cunning” and “devilish idea”:

[we should say that] this newly sprouted monster is a mere reflection [i.e., reversal] of the Western belfry type, and that this [reflection] was born out of an infantile rivalry . . . that is: because our Saint Denis (against the rules of Western architecture) will have his belfry in his rear side,37 Saint Nikodemos [decided that he] has to have his in the front. Is this not ridiculous? . . . Don’t you think that this amazing idea of mine will bring the great result that we are all striving for? Won’t this choke the foetus in the womb, and thus halt the plan of the Russian?38

Here the argument is completely reversed: while Saint Eirini has been focusing on Nikodemos’ supposed Turkishness, the Ideal Belfry argues that it is instead an imitation, or rather a superficial reaction to, Western-style building. The accusation does not entirely make sense, but the other belfries burst out in triumphant laughter and congratulate the Ideal Belfry.

The “Dialogue” ends with a twist: the introduction of the “ancient belfries [αρχαία κωδωνοστάσια] of Athens”, i.e., those of the city’s Byzantine churches. These elders put an end to the plot of all the newly or not-yet-built churches and defend Nikodemos:

We have known the Russian for nine centuries, and have seen him in many different circumstances up until the present one; but we have never seen envy or rivalry in him, apart from a feeling of shame in the face of secret plans for the destruction of humanity. Petty for the petty, stupid for the stupid, and foul for the foul. [Τα μικρά τοις μικροίς, τα μωρά τοις μωροίς και τα αισχρά τοις αισχροίς.] So, petty one, hide away your stupid and foul invention.39

This ending makes it clear that the author of the “Dialogue” approved of the new project of the bell tower. What is already evident is that they disapproved of the criticisms levelled against it and the inconclusive debates about architectural style in nineteenth-century Athens. The author’s identity remains unknown: the text is only signed with the letter “S. [Σ.]”, preceded by an obscure note:

Having accidentally found this dialogue written on an ancient piece of paper with modern letters [i.e., modern language], I publish it for the sake of curiosity [and] to make it known to all belfries.40

The author’s mention of “modern letters” on “ancient paper” reads like a satirical reference to another great debate of the time: the “Greek language question”, about whether the language of modern Greece ought to be the commonly spoken vernacular or a cultivated literary language modelled on ancient Greek. But the note also reads like a cautious (albeit joking) denial of authorship. The fact that this author felt the urge to publish their text anonymously, and to disguise their opinion as the voice of the city’s “ancient belfries”, is indicative of the tense atmosphere of Athens in the middle of the nineteenth century.

More than a piece of architectural criticism, the “Dialogue” was a symptom of the anxieties of Greek nation-building, which the Crimean War intensified: to establish a modern state and maintain alliances with Western powers, a clear connection with the classical past had to be enforced on a country whose history was marked by centuries of Byzantine and Ottoman culture as well as Christian Orthodox alliances. Medieval and vernacular architecture, which for many in the West served as the foundation of nationhood, were, in the case of Greece, highly contested. For some, Byzantium was a symbol of the local faith; for others, a source of unwanted “oriental” pedigree.

The author of the “Dialogue” was bold enough to satirize all factions involved in the political debates of the time, from the provincialism of their compatriots to the opportunism of foreign powers. And they were cautious enough to resort to anonymity and ventriloquism. At the time of the emergence of the idea of “heritage”, and as both old monuments and new projects became increasingly charged with ideological claims, one could simply let the buildings talk.

Dr. Nikos Magouliotis is an architectural historian and lecturer at ETH Zurich. His research focuses on the intersections between architecture, popular culture, archaeology, and ethnography in the east Mediterranean and in Central Europe. He has published articles in magazines such as San Rocco, ARCH+, and Platform Space, as well as papers in the following academic journals: Architectural Histories, Future Anterior, The Journal of Architecture, Architecture Beyond Europe, and OASE.
